title: High Potential for What, Exactly
author: Admired Leadership
summary: This article challenges the common organizational practice of labeling employees as "high potential" without defining potential for what. It argues that leadership potential is often conflated with other, equally valuable forms of potential, such as technical expertise, project management skill, or commercial acumen, leading organizations to fast-track people into leadership roles that don't fit their actual strengths. The author calls on organizations to explicitly define what kind of potential they're identifying and to resist assuming that every capable person should be groomed for a senior leadership track.
points: The label "high potential" is often applied without organizations clarifying potential for what specifically.
Leadership potential is frequently conflated with other valuable forms of potential, like technical or commercial skill.
Fast-tracking people into leadership roles based on unclear criteria can be a poor fit for their actual strengths.
Organizations are urged to define what kind of potential they're identifying before acting on the label.
quotes: Organizations work hard to identify those team members who possess high potential.
The idea of what counts as high potential, however, is rarely debated: Potential for what?
In many cases, those with the label rise quickly through the ranks of leadership even though their skills to lead others is not where they excel.
Not all potential reflects a prowess for leadership. Before deciding who the high potentials are, the best organizations define what they mean and who they are looking for.
Just don’t presume everyone with the ability to do more should become a more senior leader or manager.
